title: The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5
authors: de Grey, Aubrey D. N. J.
why: First finite non-4-colourable unit-distance graph; every later 5-chromatic record is a reduction of this construction.
facts: smallest exhibited graph has 1581 vertices (abstract; Fig. 9)
the wheel H has 7 vertices and 12 edges, and L contains 52 copies of H (S1 and S3)
M contains a copy of H with no 4-colouring in which that H has a monochromatic triple (S1)

title: Computing Small Unit-Distance Graphs with Chromatic Number 5
why: Turns the 1581-vertex existence proof into SAT-trimmed 553-vertex graphs with mechanically checkable proofs.
facts: produces several 553-vertex 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs (abstract)
the reduction is clausal-proof minimization applied to a 1581-vertex seed (abstract)

title: Trimming Graphs Using Clausal Proof Optimization
why: The proof-optimization method that produced the 529-vertex record; the direct predecessor of Parts' 509.
facts: reduces 553 vertices / 2720 edges to 529 vertices / 2670 edges (abstract)

title: Graph minimization, focusing on the example of 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs in the plane
why: Holds the current 509-vertex record and documents the minimization pipeline that found it.
facts: 509 vertices and 2442 edges (abstract; Table 1)
the graph splits into 374 vertices / 1860 edges plus 136 vertices / 564 edges (S6)
the previous 510-vertex graph has 2502 edges (Table 1)

title: A small 6-chromatic two-distance graph in the plane
why: A 16-vertex 6-chromatic graph for two distances; the smallest known target for a level-5 virtual edge.
facts: 16 vertices, symmetry group of order 48, 28 edges of length 1 and 28 of length d (S2)
the graph contains 5-cliques, so at least five colours are needed (proof of the main theorem)

title: The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5 - a new proof
why: Human-scale alternative to de Grey's computer construction, via a forced equal pair in G40.
facts: G40 has 40 points, 82 unit edges and 59 pairs at distance 8/3 (S2)
G79 has 79 points and 165 unit edges (S2, after Claim 2.1)

title: A 6-chromatic two-distance graph in the plane
why: The 426-vertex 6-chromatic two-distance graph, the other known target for replacing a non-unit edge.
facts: K has 426 vertices, 2009 edges of length 1 and 892 edges of length 2 (S2, after Claim 2.2)
every 5-colouring of K forces three named vertices to split (S2)

title: What percent of the plane can be properly 5- and 6-colored?
why: The tiling/density source of the 6993-vertex lower bound for 7-chromatic graphs.
facts: any unit-distance graph of order at most 6992 is 6-colourable (abstract)
any unit-distance graph of order at most 24 is 5-colourable (abstract)
the 6-colouring covers more than 99.985698% of the plane (abstract)

title: On lower bounds of the order of k-chromatic unit distance graphs
authors: de Grey, Aubrey D. N. J.
why: States the refined numerical bound used to kill the 509-plus-gadget route: v7 > 6992.
facts: v5 >= 509 and e5 >= 2406 are the corresponding upper-record data (S1)

title: The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable
why: Raises the plane lower bound to 6, leaving exactly the 6-versus-7 question; the proof is infinitary and gives no finite witness.
facts: Theorem 1.1: there is no proper 5-colouring of R^2, even with arbitrary colour classes; hence 6 <= chi(R^2) <= 7 (p. 2)
the proof works in ZFC and transfers arbitrary colourings to weak measurable ones (Theorems 1.3 and 1.4)
no finite vertex set or edge list is produced (the paper says the graph and constant are existential)

title: The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable - Lean 4 formalization
why: Machine-checked version of the infinitary theorem; also the evidence that no finite witness can be extracted from it.
facts: Five.lean is 131 lines with 0 occurrences of `sorry`
`theorem no_proper_five_coloring : not exists c : C -> Fin 5, ProperColoring 5 c` is at line 124
the file proves the statement for the continuum C, not for a finite `Fin N` vertex set

title: Planar unit distances - Lean 4 formalization of a sub-4/3 exponent
why: The unit-distance counting problem is the quantitative sibling of Hadwiger-Nelson; this is the first sub-3/2 exponent with a formal proof, not a full resolution.
facts: Main.lean is 137 lines with 0 occurrences of `sorry`
`theorem main : exists C beta : R, 0 < C and 1 <= beta and beta < 4/3 and forall n, u n <= C * n^beta` (lines 129-131)
this gives a power saving over the trivial O(n^{3/2}) bound but not the conjectured n^{1+o(1)}

title: Polymath16 wiki: Hadwiger-Nelson problem
why: The community ledger of vertex/edge counts and gadget definitions that the papers omit.
facts: table: G has 1581 vertices / 7877 edges and G0 has 1585 / 7909
L has 121 vertices / 301 edges and M has 1345 / 8268
the diamond is 4 vertices / 5 edges and the Moser spindle is 7 / 11

title: A 14-vertex 6-chromatic distance graph in the Euclidean plane (prescribed distances 1, 1/sqrt3, 2)
why: The smallest known 6-chromatic graph for three prescribed distances; a concrete calibration object below 509 vertices.
facts: G14 has 14 vertices and 50 edges: 18 of length 1, 27 of length 1/sqrt3, 5 of length 2 (README table)
chi(G14) = 6 and omega(G14) = 4; the distance triple admits no K5 anywhere in the plane (README)
no 13-point witness exists, so 14 is minimum (README, main result 3)

title: The Falconer distance conjecture in all dimensions
why: A distance-set problem in the same circle as Hadwiger-Nelson, resolved in full and with a quantitative threshold.
facts: Theorem 1.1: for every integer d >= 2 and compact E in R^d, dim_H E > d/2 implies the distance set of E has positive Lebesgue measure
the threshold d/2 is sharp and no regularity beyond Hausdorff dimension is assumed

title: Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions
why: A 2025 resolution of a major incidence/geometry conjecture; the technique (tube volume estimates) is the closest transferable machinery to distance-set bounds.
facts: every Kakeya set in R^3 has Minkowski and Hausdorff dimension 3 (abstract)

title: de Grey Graphs
why: Records the dimension-3 state of the art, where 6-chromatic graphs are explicit but 5-chromatic triangle-free examples appear only in 2026.
facts: 59- and 60-vertex unit-distance graphs in R^3 have chromatic number 6
a 61-vertex triangle-free unit-distance graph in R^3 has chromatic number 5
the plane record listed is still the 2131-vertex spindle-free graph

title: Measurable Chromatic Number of the Plane
why: The measurable variant is the standard test of whether an unrestricted colouring argument can be made geometric; Falconer's bound is its founding result.
facts: surveys the measurable chromatic number chi_m(R^2), with Falconer's 1981 lower bound chi_m(R^2) >= 5
the unrestricted and measurable numbers are not known to coincide; both lie between 5 and 7

title: Ganze Cremona-Transformationen
why: The origin of the problem: polynomial self-maps with constant non-zero Jacobian determinant.
facts: poses the question for polynomial maps F : C^n -> C^n with det JF in C*; such maps are now called Keller maps
the planar case JC(2) is still open

title: A Jacobian criterion for separability
why: The first degree bound: degree 2 is settled in every dimension, so all counterexample searches start at degree 3.
facts: every Keller map of total degree <= 2 is invertible, in every dimension (main theorem)

title: On the Jacobian conjecture and the configurations of roots
why: The degree-100 wall, the first bound obtained by Newton-polygon/root-configuration analysis.
facts: a planar Keller counterexample must have total degree > 100 (main theorem)

title: An effective approach to Keller's Jacobian Conjecture
why: Reduces the whole conjecture to cubic-linear maps, the standard finite-dimensional reduction used by later searches.
facts: reduces JC(n) to maps of the form F = x + (Ax)^{*3} with A nilpotent (cubic-linear reduction)

title: Lectures on Expansion Techniques in Algebraic Geometry
why: The valuation/Newton-polygon dictionary for Keller pairs; the source of the two-points-at-infinity constraint.
facts: Theorem (19.4): JC is equivalent to each of k[f,g]=A, f having one point at infinity, N(f) being a triangle, and deg f | deg g or deg g | deg f
every component of a Keller pair has at most two points at infinity (Theorem 18.13, used in 19.4)

title: Polynomial derivations and their rings of constants
why: The derivation-side formulation: rings of constants and the local nilpotence criteria that make JC equivalent to a statement about derivations.
facts: monograph (1994) on derivations of k[x_1,...,x_n] and their rings of constants
the Nowicki conjecture on Weitzenboeck derivations is posed in this setting

title: Polynomial Automorphisms and the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The standard monograph: normal forms, reductions, and the equivalence list that every Jacobian search uses.
facts: second edition, Frontiers in Mathematics (Birkhaeuser, 2021); first edition 2000
the monograph treats Keller maps, the degree reduction, and the derivation/Dixmier reformulations

title: A reduction of the Jacobian Conjecture to the symmetric case
why: Shows the conjecture can be tested on symmetric Jacobian matrices, shrinking the coefficient space of any search.
facts: reduces JC to the case in which the Jacobian matrix is symmetric (main theorem)

title: Some algorithms related to the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The only published Newton-polygon corner enumerator; it defines the admissible search space below degree 150.
facts: enumerates all possible corners for gcd(deg P, deg Q) <= 35 (abstract)
enumerates all degree pairs with max(deg P, deg Q) <= 150 (abstract)

title: Increasing the degree of a possible counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture from 100 to 108
why: The (72,108) reduction: below degree 125 only this pair survives, with exactly two Newton-polygon configurations.
facts: Theorem 2.1: max{deg P, deg Q} >= 125, or (deg P, deg Q) is (72,108) or (108,72) (p. 3)
Proposition 4.3 lists exactly two configurations: N(P)={(0,0),(1,0),(8,14),(8,16),(0,8)} and N(Q)={(0,0),(2,1),(12,21),(12,24),(0,12)} for (1), and the four-corner versions for (2) (p. 23)
the proved lower bound rises from 100 to 108, not to 125 (abstract)

title: The Alpoge-Fable counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture: verification, geometry, dynamics, and an equivariant program for the plane case
why: Independent verification and geometric analysis of the July 2026 C^3 counterexample; the reference object for the non-planar case.
facts: records an independent verification of the July 2026 polynomial map C^3 -> C^3 with constant non-zero determinant and a three-point collision
the associated note is jacobian-note-v1.1.pdf (273 kB) with a Python verification repository

title: A digestion of the Jacobian conjecture counterexample
why: The clearest derivation of where the C^3 map comes from; documents the degree and determinant data an auditor needs.
facts: the map has component degrees 7, 6 and 4 and total degree 7
the Jacobian determinant is the constant -2, so a linear change of one component normalises it to 1
the generic fibre has three points

title: The new counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture
why: The algebraic-geometry reading of the counterexample, including the collision and the monodromy computation.
facts: gives explicit rational collision points for the C^3 map
records a separate 2026 cubic-homogeneous map in 24 variables with det(DG) = 1 and a rational collision (announced in the comments)

title: The plane (72,108) Jacobian case - an independent structural proof
why: Claims to close both (72,108) configurations, which would raise the plane degree bound to 125; unrefereed but with executable checkers.
facts: Theorem A: no (P,Q) in K[x,x^-1,y]^2 with [P,Q]=x^2 and either configuration (1) or configuration (2) of GGHV 2022, Proposition 4.3
Corollary B: conditional on two stated inputs, every plane counterexample has max{deg P, deg Q} >= 125
the README attributes priority for the exclusion to Helali, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21479814

title: Jacobian conjecture, two-dimensional case
why: A complete classification of planar Keller pairs of total degree at most 3, which makes the low-degree box provably empty.
facts: classifies all Keller pairs of total degree <= 3 up to linear conjugacy (main theorem)
the normal form is (x + a2 s^2 + a3 s^3, y - a2 s^2 - a3 s^3) with s = x+y and determinant 1

title: Structure of Keller mappings, two-dimensional case
why: Extends the classification to degree 4 and exhibits the first non-triangular tame families, calibrating what a counterexample must not look like.
facts: classifies Keller pairs of total degree <= 4 (main theorem)
exhibits F_{c,s} = (x + c y^2, y - s x^2 - 2cs x y^2 - c^2 s y^4) with c,s non-zero and determinant 1

title: Some classes satisfying the 2-dimensional Jacobian conjecture and a proof of the complex conjecture until degree 104
why: The current unconditional degree wall for JC(2): 104, four above Moh's 100.
facts: proves the complex two-dimensional Jacobian conjecture for total degree <= 104 (abstract)
improves Moh's 1983 bound of 100 (abstract)

title: Sur les algebres de Weyl
why: The non-commutative sibling: endomorphisms of the Weyl algebra, equivalent to JC in the stable range and open in every dimension.
facts: poses the endomorphism problem for the Weyl algebra A_n(C)
Dixmier(n) is equivalent to JC(n) for the same n (Tsuchimoto; Belov-Kanel-Kontsevich)

title: A Dimension-Two Counterexample to the Separable Jacobian Conjecture in Characteristic Two
why: A clean solved analogue: the separable Jacobian conjecture is false in characteristic 2, in dimension 2, with an explicit degree-3 collision.
facts: over the algebraic closure of F_2, F = (x + x^2 y + x^4 + x^6 y^2, y + x^5 + x^6 y + x^7 y^2 + x^8 y^3) has det JF = 1
the three distinct points (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) have the same image
the function-field extension has degree 3 and is separable

title: The tame and the wild automorphisms of polynomial rings in three variables
why: A solved structural analogue: the tame generators problem, open for decades, was settled negatively in dimension 3.
facts: proves that Aut(k[x,y,z]) contains wild automorphisms (main theorem)
the tame generators problem has a negative answer in dimension 3

title: Mathieu-Zhao Spaces and the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The Mathieu-Zhao reformulation is the widest currently open statement that JC is known to imply.
facts: introduces Mathieu-Zhao subspaces and connects them to the Mathieu conjecture (2020 survey chapter)
JC implies the Mathieu conjecture for the appropriate class of maps

title: A proof of the two-dimensional Markus-Yamabe Stability Conjecture and a generalization
why: The dynamical analogue of JC(2) that *is* true: a global-stability statement for planar polynomial vector fields.
facts: proves the Markus-Yamabe conjecture in dimension 2: a local diffeomorphism of R^2 whose Jacobian has negative trace everywhere has 0 as a global attractor (abstract)

title: A Polynomial Counterexample to the Markus-Yamabe Conjecture
why: Shows the dimension-2 Markus-Yamabe theorem does not lift: the polynomial counterexample appears already in dimension 3.
facts: exhibits a polynomial counterexample to Markus-Yamabe in dimension 3
the planar theorem therefore does not generalise to n >= 3

title: Notes on elliptic curves. II.
why: The conjecture itself, in the form the terminal object must refute: analytic order of vanishing equals Mordell-Weil rank.
facts: conjecture: ord_{s=1} L(E,s) = rank E(Q)
the leading coefficient is predicted as a product of the real period, regulator, |Sha|, Tamagawa numbers and torsion

title: Heegner points and derivatives of L-series
why: The rank-1 half of BSD: the first derivative is an explicit multiple of the height of a Heegner point.
facts: proves L'(E,1) equals an explicit non-zero constant times the canonical height of a Heegner point (rank 1)
together with the rank-0 case this gives BSD for analytic rank <= 1 once Sha is controlled

title: Euler Systems
why: The other half of Gross-Zagier-Kolyvagin: an Euler system bounds the Selmer group, so analytic rank <= 1 forces the algebraic rank.
facts: introduces Euler systems and applies them to Heegner points on modular elliptic curves
for analytic rank <= 1, the Mordell-Weil rank equals the analytic rank and Sha is finite

title: Explicit Heegner Points: Kolyvagin's Conjecture and Non-trivial Elements in the Shafarevich-Tate Group
why: The precise citation for the GZK gate and for the rank >= 2 Selmer corank statement that rules out the easy counterexample shapes.
facts: Theorem 1.1 (Gross-Zagier, Kolyvagin): if r_an(E/Q) <= 1 then r_an(E/Q) = r_MW(E/Q) (p. 3)
Kolyvagin's conjecture implies that analytic rank >= 2 forces Z_p-corank Sel_p >= 2 (abstract)

title: Proving the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for specific elliptic curves of analytic rank zero and one
why: The largest published pointwise verification in the GZK range; calibrates how far 'checked' actually extends.
facts: proves BSD for 16,714 of the 16,725 curves of conductor < 5000 with analytic rank 0 or 1 (abstract)

title: LMFDB - Reliability of L-function data
why: Establishes that analytic ranks above 1 are rigorously certified in the database, which invalidates 'k >= 2 is not certifiable'.
facts: for classical modular form L-functions the displayed analytic rank has been rigorously verified in all cases, including rank > 1 (page text)
for any displayed analytic rank r <= 1 the value must be correct (page text)

title: LMFDB - Completeness of elliptic curve data over Q
why: Defines the region where a rank mismatch is impossible by construction, and hence the only region worth sweeping.
facts: the database contains all curves of conductor < 500,000 (page text)
it contains 3,824,372 curves in 2,917,287 isogeny classes, with maximum conductor 299,996,953 (page text)
it also contains all 7-smooth conductors and all prime conductors <= 300,000,000

title: Elliptic curves by rank
why: The rank-record tables that supply calibration curves for any certified-rank pipeline.
facts: rank 4 record: conductor 234,446, curve [1,-1,0,-79,289]
rank 5 record: conductor 19,047,851, curve [0,0,1,-79,342]
rank 6 record: conductor 5,187,563,742, curve [1,1,0,-2582,48720]

title: Curves D y^2 = x^3 - x of odd analytic rank
why: A large explicit family where odd analytic rank is proved and BSD then predicts positive rank; the standard congruent-number computation.
facts: proves positive rank for every |D| < 10^6 with |D| congruent to 5, 6 or 7 mod 8 (abstract)
the proof uses Heegner points from CM points on modular curves and a numerical height check

title: Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves
why: The strongest unconditional average-rank bound; it is why a random curve is not where a counterexample will be found.
facts: the mean size of the 2-Selmer group, ordered by height, is 3 (abstract)
consequently limsup of the average rank is at most 1.5 (abstract)

title: The class number of quadratic fields and the conjectures of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer
why: The bridge that made the class-number problem a corollary of an analytic-rank statement, later closed by Gross-Zagier.
facts: reduces the effective class-number problem for imaginary quadratic fields to the existence of an elliptic curve with a zero of order >= 3 at s = 1
Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa, series 4, volume 3 (1976), pages 623-663

title: Congruent Numbers and Heegner Points
why: The congruent-number problem is the cleanest conditional corollary of BSD; Tian's Heegner-point construction gives unconditional families.
facts: constructs Heegner points on m y^2 = x^3 - x for integers m with many prime divisors (abstract)
extends Heegner's prime-conductor construction to composite m

title: A Family of Calabi-Yau Varieties and Potential Automorphy II
why: Sato-Tate is the model 'local-statistics' theorem: a conjecture about every elliptic curve, proved by potential automorphy.
facts: proves potential automorphy for a family of Calabi-Yau varieties (main theorem)
this yields the Sato-Tate conjecture for elliptic curves over Q

title: Modular Elliptic Curves and Fermat's Last Theorem
why: The canonical 'big theorem with a complete method' case: modularity of semistable curves, then FLT as a corollary.
facts: proves that every semistable elliptic curve over Q is modular (main theorem)
deduces Fermat's Last Theorem for all exponents >= 3

title: The DRAT format and DRAT-trim checker
why: The certificate format behind every claimed unit-distance lower bound; a SAT answer without a DRAT/LRAT trace is not a proof.
facts: DRAT extends RUP with the RAT rule and is checkable in polynomial time per step (abstract)
DRAT-trim is the reference checker described in the paper

title: Computational methods and experiments in analytic number theory
why: The practical reference for the approximate functional equation and for rigorous zero-counting of L-functions.
facts: surveys the approximate functional equation, smoothed sums and zero-counting for L-functions
the worked examples include large-scale verification of the Riemann hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions

title: Computing special values of motivic L-functions
why: The algorithm that turns a functional equation into certified numerical L-values and Taylor coefficients.
facts: computes L-values and Taylor coefficients from a smoothed approximate functional equation (abstract)
the method applies to motivic L-functions with a known functional equation

title: Arb: Efficient Arbitrary-Precision Midpoint-Radius Interval Arithmetic
why: The interval backend that makes a numerical analytic rank into a certified statement rather than a tolerance test.
facts: implements midpoint-radius interval arithmetic with rigorous error bounds (abstract)
supports arbitrary-precision special functions used in L-function evaluation
